question: For the outermost regions and many of our partner countries, particularly in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific region (ACP countries), the banana sector is a responsible and structural part of the economy and one which is committed to the green transition.

However, the sector faces overwhelming and growing competition from South American dollar bananas, which account for 75% of bananas on the European market and benefit from social and environmental standards that are less strict than European standards.

Through the Partnership Agreement with the countries of South and Central America, the Commission had negotiated a stabilisation mechanism for the banana sector, which has now expired. This mechanism allowed for the temporary suspension of trade preferences when an import threshold was exceeded.
Despite the thresholds being repeatedly exceeded, it has never been triggered, to the detriment of the EU and ACP banana sectors. 1.
Is the Commission committed to taking measures to safeguard EU and ACP banana producers?
Will it also undertake to maintain the customs duty on Latin American producers, which amounts to EUR 75 per tonne exported to the European market?
What other measures does it intend to introduce in favour of European sectors to address this growing competitive asymmetry?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.3.2024) The Commission is aware of the importance of the banana sector for the outermost regions and African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States (ACP) countries and treats banana as a sensitive product in all trade negotiations to maintain a balanced market. Only least developed and ACP countries have duty-free quota-free access to the EU market.

In trade agreements, banana exporting countries are granted access through partial tariff liberalisation at the level of EUR 75 per tonne. In 2019, both the Andean Community as well as the Central America countries requested the EU to carry out a review of the preferential tariff for bananas, as foreseen in the respective trade agreements.

This review resulted in no change to the preferential tariff for bananas from these countries, which remains at the level of EUR 75 per tonne. The same tariff has also been agreed with Mercosur and with Mexico (in the modernised trade agreement). EU trade agreements also have Trade and Sustainable Development Chapters1, including with Latin American countries.

These contain legally binding commitments to uphold high environmental and labour standards and to effectively implement international agreements in that respect. The EU works to make sure that those standards are respected. In addition, European banana producers are supported under the Programme of options specifically relating to remoteness and insularity (POSEI)2.

For the banana sector, in 2022, France allocated an annual amount of EUR 129.1 million, Spain (the Canary Islands) EUR 141.1 million and Portugal EUR 8.7 million. The total annual amount for the banana sector was EUR 278.9 million (42.7% of the total POSEI allocation).
1 Sustainable development in EU trade agreements, https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/development-and-

sustainability/sustainable-development/sustainable-development-eu-trade-agreements_en 2 Programme of options specifically relating to remoteness and insularity (first pillar of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) financed by the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF)) replacing the direct payments granted under the first pillar of the CAP in all other EU regions.
